Normal: Warm, but modern processors are designed to run here under load — this is only worth acting on if it stays high while the PC is idle.
If it is hot at idle: clean dust from the heatsink and fans, and check the CPU cooler is properly seated.
Bad: At this temperature the CPU will be reducing its own speed to protect itself, so the PC feels slower than it should.
Clean dust from the cooler and case filters, make sure intake and exhaust fans are working, and check the cooler is firmly mounted.
If the cooler was never re-pasted and the PC is several years old, fresh thermal paste often drops temperatures substantially.
Turn off any CPU overclock while diagnosing.

rules.forecast: Sustained heat shortens the life of every component near it, and thermal shutdowns risk file-system damage.

Normal: Warm near the processor. Normal under heavy load; if it stays this high while the PC is doing little, dust or old thermal paste is the usual cause.
This is the motherboard's sensor, not the processor's own. Installing PawnIO lets the app read the processor directly.
Bad: Very hot near the processor. At this level the processor slows itself down to protect itself, so the PC feels slower than it should.
Clean the fan and heatsink. On a laptop several years old, fresh thermal paste often lowers temperatures a lot.
Check the charger is the wattage the laptop needs: an underpowered charger can also hold the processor back.

rules.forecast: Sustained heat shortens the life of every component near it, and thermal shutdowns risk file-system damage.

Normal: Normal for a graphics card under load. Worth improving case airflow if it sits here while idle.
Bad: The card is running hot enough to throttle. Clean dust from its fans and heatsink, and improve case airflow.
Check that nothing is blocking the card's intake, and that its fans actually spin up under load.

Normal: The hot spot runs warmer than the core by design; keep an eye on it if the gap keeps widening.
Bad: A very high hot spot, especially when the core temperature looks fine, usually means poor contact between the GPU die and its cooler — degraded thermal paste or pads, or an uneven mount.
On an older card, a repaste is the usual fix. If it is under warranty, contact the manufacturer instead.

Normal: Graphics memory tolerates high temperatures, but improving case airflow will help it last.
Bad: Memory temperature is at the level where the card starts throttling to protect itself. Improve case airflow and clean the card.
On cards several years old, the thermal pads over the memory are a common culprit and can be replaced.
Hardware is warm but no fan reports any speed. Check that fan cables are connected, and listen for a fan that has seized.
A stopped fan on a warm system leads to throttling and, eventually, heat damage — fix this before doing anything demanding.

Normal: Memory was fairly full while scanning. If the PC often feels slow, closing browser tabs or adding RAM would help.
Bad: Memory was nearly exhausted, which forces Windows to page to disk and makes everything feel slow.
Close what you are not using and re-check; if it is always this full, more RAM is the real fix.
